proposal: The Mandate recommends that the USAID Administrator also serve as Director of Foreign Assistance at State with the rank of Deputy Secretary, overseeing all US foreign assistance, and that the Administration evaluate and consolidate the foreign assistance authorities spread across roughly 20 offices and agencies. It envisions USAID continuing as an agency, with political appointees in key posts and its policy functions reorganized.

status_summary: Executive Order 14169 (signed 2025-01-20) paused foreign development assistance for a 90-day review, State told Congress on 2025-03-28 that it would absorb USAID functions, and NPR reported that USAID shut down on 2025-07-01 with a few hundred remaining employees merged into State. State then placed the powers of the Director of Foreign Assistance and five other State aid-related offices under an Under Secretary for Foreign Assistance, Humanitarian Affairs, and Religious Freedom (Delegation of Authority No. 597, signed 2025-08-21, replaced by No. 597-1 on 2026-03-13). This follows the Mandate's aim of aligning aid with State but differs in design: the lead official is an Under Secretary rather than a Deputy Secretary-rank dual-hatted USAID Administrator, and the agency was wound down rather than kept. No statute abolishing USAID was found, and a State delegation signed 2026-09-18 and published 2026-10-02 gives the official performing the Administrator's duties authority over closeout and wind-down funds through 2027-06-30. Whether aid authorities held by agencies outside State have been consolidated was not found.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14169 directs agency heads to halt new obligations and disbursements of foreign development assistance for 90 days pending program-by-program review for consistency with US foreign policy, with State and OMB controlling resumption (published 2025-01-30).

State announces it is officially shutting down USAID's independent operations and tells Congress it plans to reorganize some USAID functions within the department by 2025-07-01; experts quoted say dissolving an agency would normally need congressional approval. The same day a Fourth Circuit panel stays a district court ruling that the dismantling was likely unconstitutional.

USAID officially shuts down; a few hundred remaining employees merge into the State Department, which begins managing the programs the administration chose to keep. NPR reported that more than 80% of USAID programs had been terminated.

State publishes Delegation of Authority No. 597 (signed 2025-08-21), moving to the Under Secretary for Foreign Assistance, Humanitarian Affairs, and Religious Freedom the powers of the Director of Foreign Assistance and the heads of State's refugee, democracy and human rights, global HIV/AIDS, global health security and stabilization offices.

The FY2026 appropriations act (Public Law 119-75, signed 2026-02-03; Division F is the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act) provides about 50.07 billion dollars net of rescissions, including 5.40 billion dollars for a new International Humanitarian Assistance account that carries the authorities of the former International Disaster Assistance and Migration and Refugee Assistance accounts (per CRS). CRS does not describe USAID as abolished; it notes that the Administration sought to transition select USAID functions to State and to phase out others.

State publishes Delegation of Authority No. 597-1 (signed 2026-03-13), which replaces No. 597 and adds the Assistant Secretary for Disaster and Humanitarian Response to the offices whose authorities the Under Secretary holds; a companion delegation (No. 619) gives that Assistant Secretary the Secretary's disaster assistance, global food security and humanitarian response authorities.
State's FY2027 budget justification requests over $21 million for 400 employees hired in 2025 to absorb USAID functions, as reported by Federal News Network (month-only date).

State publishes Delegation of Authority No. 634 (signed 2026-09-18), giving the official performing the duties of the USAID Administrator authority to approve and spend funds for closing out USAID awards and winding down its functions, with reports to the Under Secretary every two months, through 2027-06-30.

title: Put foreign assistance under State leadership and restructure USAID
uncertainties: Litigation outcomes (Does v. Musk, AFSA v. Trump and related cases) were searched twice and only 2025 coverage was returned, so the current state of those cases is not stated beyond the 2025-03-28 stay. Whether USAID is legally abolished is not settled by any document opened for this record. An unverified lead from an encyclopedia page (Wikipedia, low confidence, pending official documentation) says that abolition needs an act of Congress, and the ABC7 News report of 2025-03-28 in the record quotes experts to similar effect; the 2026-09-18 delegation still refers to an official performing the Administrator's duties, and CRS report R48624 does not describe the agency as abolished. The text of the FY2026 appropriations act on USAID was not read in full (the GovInfo copy of Public Law 119-75 was opened, but its State and foreign operations division was not reached). The FY2026 appropriations act is described here through CRS report R48624, not through its own Division F text. The Mandate's consolidation of authorities spread across about twenty offices and agencies, outside State, was not researched. An unverified lead from an encyclopedia page (Wikipedia, low confidence) cites an October 2026 Reuters report that USAID is expected to disband; a search for that report found nothing, and neither it nor any official document confirming the claim was opened. Federal Register pages for Delegations of Authority No. 597 (90 FR 43020), No. 597-1 (91 FR 13927) and No. 634 (91 FR 62802) and the API record for Executive Order 14169 (90 FR 8619) were opened and match the record; No. 597 states no separate effective date. The State Department's own reorganization documents and the 2025-03-28 congressional notification (state.gov) were not opened, and one search for the Fourth Circuit outcome in the USAID dismantling suits returned only 2025 coverage.
